claim: The budget cap is compared with spend only after each model response arrives, so a run can exceed max_budget_usd by the cost of the response that crossed it plus whatever still-running background subagents spend before they stop.
why: Each response's cost is only known from the token usage the API returns with it.
check: Check that a runner sets the cap below the real hard limit it must honor, leaving headroom for one response and running subagents; a cap equal to the hard limit is a problem.
quote: Spend can therefore pass the cap by up to the cost of that one response, plus anything that subagents still running at that moment spend before they stop.

claim: max_turns and max_budget_usd both default to no limit, and the docs say setting a budget is a good default for production agents because open-ended prompts can run long.
why: Without limits the loop runs until Claude finishes on its own.
check: Check whether production agents running open-ended prompts set a spend budget.
quote: Without limits, the loop runs until Claude finishes on its own, which is fine for well-scoped tasks but can run long on open-ended prompts ("improve this codebase"). Setting a budget is a good default for production agents.

claim: A run that hits max_turns or max_budget_usd ends with a ResultMessage of subtype error_max_turns or error_max_budget_usd that has no result field, and max_turns counts each tool-calling turn plus one final text-only turn.
why: A turn cap that covers only the tool-calling turns leaves no turn for the final response.
check: Check that the runner branches on the result subtype before reading the result text, and that its turn cap leaves one turn beyond the expected tool turns; reading result on an error subtype would be a bug.
quote: Count each turn with tool calls, plus one for the final text-only response. Without that extra turn, the run ends with a `ResultMessage` of subtype `error_max_turns` and no final response.

claim: A single-shot query() raises after yielding an error result and the underlying Claude Code process exits with a nonzero code, while a streaming-input session stays alive except after a session crash.
why: The SDK yields the error result first, so callers can capture total_cost_usd, usage, num_turns and session_id before handling the exception.
check: Check that a runner wraps the query loop so the cost and session_id from an error result are still recorded; losing them on max-turns or max-budget exits is a problem.
quote: A single-shot `query()` call yields the final result message, then raises an error that includes the failure text, such as `Reached maximum number of turns`. The raise is intentional. Wrap the loop in a try block if your code needs to continue past it. The underlying Claude Code process also exits with a nonzero code.

claim: After a session crash the final result is an error_during_execution whose cost fields may be zeroed and whose stop_reason is null, and the process exits after emitting it.
why: The crash result is synthesized by Claude Code rather than produced by the loop, so its totals are not reliable.
check: If a runner sums cost from result messages, check that it treats a zeroed crash result as incomplete accounting and uses earlier messages for whatever usage can be recovered.
quote: After a session crash, the final result is an `error_during_execution` whose cost fields may be zeroed and whose `stop_reason` is `null`, and the process exits after emitting it.

claim: --resume by session ID searches the current project directory and its git worktrees and then every other project on the machine, and also accepts the absolute path of a session .jsonl transcript.
why: Before v2.1.223 the ID search covered only the current project directory and its git worktrees.
check: If a runner relies on cross-project resume by session ID, check that it runs Claude Code v2.1.223 or later.
quote: When you pass a session ID, Claude Code searches the current project directory and its git worktrees, then every other project on this machine. Before v2.1.223, the ID search covered only the current project directory and its git worktrees.

claim: By default the system prompt is built once on a conversation's first request and recorded in the session, so different system prompt flags passed on a later --resume or --continue take effect only after compaction or in a new conversation.
why: The recorded prompt can keep supplying the launch-time instructions even after --resume or --continue.
check: If a runner with system prompt recording enabled changes --append-system-prompt when resuming, check whether it expects the new text before compaction without passing --system-prompt-snapshot off.
quote: Until the conversation is compacted, every later request uses that recorded prompt, including after you return to the conversation with `--resume` or `--continue`. If you pass different system prompt flag text, or none, on that later launch, it takes effect once the conversation is compacted or when you start a new conversation.

claim: Outside cloud sessions, bare mode (--bare or CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE=1) leaves system prompt recording off unless --system-prompt-snapshot on is passed, so a bare resumed run with recording off rebuilds the prompt from its current flags.
why: Bare mode skips the recording that normal mode does on the first request.
check: If a runner outside cloud sessions combines --bare with resume and expects to reuse the recorded system prompt, check whether it passes --system-prompt-snapshot on.
quote: Outside of [cloud sessions](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cloud-environments.md), if you start Claude Code in [bare mode](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless.md#start-faster-with-bare-mode) by passing `--bare` or setting `CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE=1`, recording stays off unless you pass `--system-prompt-snapshot on`.

claim: --exclude-dynamic-system-prompt-sections moves per-user context such as the auto memory location from the system prompt into the first user message, improving prompt-cache reuse across users and machines, and is ignored when --system-prompt or --system-prompt-file is set.
why: Moving per-user text out of the default system prompt reduces variation in the cached prompt across users and machines.
check: For scripted multi-user workloads running the same task with the default system prompt, check whether per-user prompt text is limiting cache reuse and whether the flag is enabled.
quote: Move per-user context, such as the auto memory location, out of the system prompt and into the first user message. Improves prompt-cache reuse across different users and machines running the same task. Only applies with the default system prompt; ignored when `--system-prompt` or `--system-prompt-file` is set.

claim: In configurations that support the split, a custom replacement system prompt can use a line containing only __SYSTEM_PROMPT_DYNAMIC_BOUNDARY__ to keep the static part above cached while the per-run part below changes (v2.1.275+).
why: The boundary lets the fixed instructions stay cached as the per-run context changes.
check: If a runner expects to cache fixed instructions separately from per-run context in a replacement system prompt, check that its configuration supports the split and that the boundary follows the fixed instructions.
quote: add a line containing only `__SYSTEM_PROMPT_DYNAMIC_BOUNDARY__` between the instructions and the context. Claude Code splits the prompt at the first such line and removes that line, so the part above it stays cached while the part below changes.

claim: With --disallowedTools, a bare rule removes matching tools and a scoped rule denies only matching calls, with EndConversation staying available while any other tool remains.
why: A scoped deny leaves the tool in Claude's context for calls outside the rule.
check: If a runner expects a tool to be unavailable, check for a bare deny rule and account for EndConversation while any other tool remains.
quote: A bare tool name removes the matching tools from Claude's context: `"Edit"` removes Edit, `"*"` removes every tool, and `"mcp__*"` removes every MCP tool. A scoped rule such as `Bash(rm *)` leaves the tool available and denies only calls that match [as written](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions.md#bash-rule-limits).

claim: In the SDK, allowed_tools auto-approves the listed tools but unlisted tools remain available, and calls to them that need approval fall through to the permission mode and canUseTool; in default mode with no canUseTool callback the call is denied.
why: allowed_tools is an approval list, not a tool whitelist.
check: If a runner wants a closed toolset, check tools for built-in availability and disallowed_tools for tools it must block, and check that a default-mode run without a callback does not expect to prompt anyone.
quote: Tools not listed are still available, and calls to them that need approval fall through to the permission mode and `canUseTool`.

claim: Without --forward-subagent-text (or CLAUDE_CODE_FORWARD_SUBAGENT_TEXT) the stream-json output omits the text and thinking blocks of foreground subagents; with it they appear as assistant and user messages with parent_tool_use_id set.
why: The flag lets a consumer reconstruct each subagent's transcript from the stream.
check: If a reviewer needs foreground subagents' text and thinking in the stream-json log, check that forwarding is enabled on a supported version.
quote: Without this flag, Claude Code omits the text and thinking blocks of a subagent that runs in the [foreground](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents.md#run-subagents-in-foreground-or-background).

claim: --no-session-persistence (print mode only) keeps the session off disk so it cannot be resumed.
why: With session persistence disabled, a later --resume or --continue has no saved session to load.
check: Check that a print-mode runner which needs to resume the run or inspect its saved session transcript does not pass --no-session-persistence.
quote: Disable session persistence so sessions are not saved to disk and cannot be resumed. Print mode only.

claim: From Claude Code v2.1.221, -p with --mcp-config waits before the first turn for pending MCP servers without cached tool lists, up to MCP_TIMEOUT (30 seconds by default) or a shorter limit in self-hosted environments.
why: Servers with cached tool lists skip the wait and connect on first use.
check: Check that the runner's startup timeout allows for pending MCP connections under its hosting and cache configuration.
quote: When you pass this flag with `-p`, Claude Code waits for still-pending servers to connect before running the first turn, up to the [`MCP_TIMEOUT`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars) startup timeout, 30 seconds by default; a server with a [cached tool list](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp.md#managing-your-servers) skips the wait and connects on first use.

claim: --settings overrides keys from settings.json files for the session but most list-valued settings merge with the file-based values, and omitted keys keep their file values; the file must be a regular file no larger than 2 MiB.
why: The flag layers on top of existing settings rather than replacing them.
check: If a runner uses --settings to narrow permissions or disable hooks, check whether omitted keys or merged lists retain entries from file-based settings.
quote: Values you set here override the same keys in your `settings.json` files for this session, but [most lists merge](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings.md#lists-merge-instead-of-overriding) with theirs. Keys you omit keep their file-based values.

claim: --max-budget-usd stops a print-mode run against a client-side cost estimate, counts subagent spend, can be overshot, and does not carry earlier spend over when a run is resumed with --continue or --resume.
why: The cap is checked against Claude Code's own estimate rather than the bill, and totals restored from earlier runs are excluded, so each resumed invocation gets a fresh allowance.
check: In a runner that resumes sessions, check whether it tracks cumulative spend separately when it needs a per-task estimate, since --max-budget-usd excludes restored totals.
quote: When you return to a conversation with `--continue` or `--resume`, totals [restored from earlier runs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/cost-tracking.md#accumulate-costs-across-multiple-calls) don't count toward it.

claim: --continue skips sessions created with claude -p or the Agent SDK (and sessions whose first prompt was /loop), whereas claude -p --continue includes them.
why: --continue selects the most recent eligible conversation for the current directory.
check: If a runner must resume a particular headless session, check that it uses the session ID or has verified that it is the most recent eligible session for -p --continue.
quote: Skips sessions created with `claude -p` or the Agent SDK, and sessions whose first prompt was `/loop`. `claude -p --continue` includes `-p`, SDK, and `/loop` sessions.

claim: Forking an SDK session branches only the conversation history, not the filesystem: edits made by a forked agent are real and visible to every session working in the same directory.
why: Sessions persist the conversation, so two forks of one session in one directory can overwrite each other's file changes.
check: If a workflow requires file changes in one fork to stay separate from another session, check whether the forks share a working directory or have separate checkouts.
quote: Forking branches the conversation history, not the filesystem. If a forked agent edits files, those changes are real and visible to any session working in the same directory.

claim: The session_id is present on every SDK result message whether the run succeeded or failed, so a run that hit error_max_turns or error_max_budget_usd can be resumed with a higher limit.
why: The docs list recovering from a limit as a standard reason to resume.
check: If a runner needs to resume limit-stopped runs, check that it stores session_id from error results and raises the limit when resuming.
quote: which is present on every result regardless of success or error.

claim: To disable SDK session persistence, set persistSession: false in TypeScript to keep the session in memory for the call, or set CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_PROMPT_HISTORY in Python's env option to suppress transcript writes.
why: The persistSession option is TypeScript only.
check: If a Python runner needs to suppress session transcript writes, check whether it sets CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_PROMPT_HISTORY in the env option.
quote: Set [`persistSession: false`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/typescript#options) (TypeScript only). The session exists only in memory for the duration of the call. In Python, set [`CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_PROMPT_HISTORY`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars) in the `env` option to suppress transcript writes instead.

claim: --restricted starts Claude Code for evaluation harnesses on shared machines: it removes command-running tools and WebFetch unless named in --tools, confines file tools to the working directories, loads only managed settings and --settings, and refuses bypassPermissions (v2.1.248+).
why: Restricted mode is intended for a shared-machine evaluation harness that needs to keep Claude Code from running commands or reading the machine's user and project settings.
check: If a shared-machine evaluation harness relies on --restricted to keep commands unavailable, check that --tools does not explicitly add back command-running built-ins.
quote: Claude Code removes the built-in tools that run commands or code, and WebFetch, unless you name them individually in `--tools`, not through the `default` preset.

claim: Continue resumes the most recent session in the current directory without an ID, so it suits one conversation at a time; resume needs the specific session ID and is required when several sessions share a directory.
why: Continue picks by recency in the working directory, which may select a different session when conversations are interleaved.
check: Check that a runner managing several conversations in one directory uses a captured session ID when it needs to return to a specific conversation.
quote: Required when you have multiple sessions (for example, one per user in a multi-user app) or want to return to one that isn't the most recent.

claim: SDK session transcripts are local files under ~/.claude/projects/<encoded-cwd>/ (or $CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/projects/), so resuming on another host requires a session store adapter with a matching cwd or a restored transcript file, while a fresh session can use captured results instead.
why: Session files are local to the machine that created them, and the docs say passing captured results into a fresh prompt is often more robust than shipping transcripts.
check: If an ephemeral runner needs to resume a session on another host, check that it can retrieve the transcript from a session store with the matching cwd or restore the file on the new host.
quote: Attach a [`sessionStore` / `session_store` adapter](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/session-storage) so the SDK mirrors transcripts to your own backend and another host can resume them. The store lookup key derives from the working directory, so resume from a `cwd` matching the original run's.

claim: total_cost_usd and costUSD are client-side estimates from a price table bundled at build time unless a modelPricing table is in effect, and the docs say not to bill end users or trigger financial decisions from these fields.
why: They drift when pricing changes, when the installed SDK does not recognize a model, or when billing rules apply that the client cannot model.
check: Check that a runner uses authoritative billing data for charge-back or financial decisions and reserves total_cost_usd for insight and approximate budgeting.
quote: The `total_cost_usd` and `costUSD` fields are client-side estimates, not authoritative billing data. The SDK computes them locally from a price table bundled at build time, unless a [`modelPricing`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#modelpricing) table is in effect.

claim: From Claude Code v2.1.277, an SDK call that resumes a session includes the earlier spend saved in the transcript in total_cost_usd, so use the latest result for the recorded session total to avoid double-counting restored spend.
why: Claude Code saves session totals to the transcript when the process exits normally and restores them on resume or fork; before v2.1.277 a resumed session started its totals at zero.
check: Check that a runner avoids summing restored spend across resumes or forks, and that it adds results from pre-v2.1.277 resumed calls when it needs a total across those calls.
quote: Each result already includes the session's earlier spend. Read the latest result for the session total; summing results double-counts the restored spend.

claim: The result-level usage field excludes subagent tokens and undercounts as soon as subagents nest, whereas total_cost_usd and modelUsage include subagent requests; on error_max_budget_usd, usage also leaves out the response that crossed the budget.
why: usage counts only the top-level agent loop.
check: Check that a runner reporting whole-tree tokens uses modelUsage or model_usage, and that a spend report uses total_cost_usd or the per-model costs.
quote: Use `modelUsage`, or `model_usage` in Python, for whole-tree token accounting; the `usage` field undercounts as soon as nesting occurs.

claim: Per-step output_tokens on assistant messages is only a placeholder taken at message_start, so output token counts must be read from the result message's usage or modelUsage rather than summed from assistant messages.
why: The real output count arrives at the end of the response and is added only to the result message.
check: Check that a runner reads output tokens from result messages instead of using assistant-message output_tokens as final counts.
quote: so the message's `output_tokens` is only the count the API had reported at `message_start`, before the response was generated.

claim: In streaming input mode each turn emits its own result whose total_cost_usd is the running total for the call, and /clear, /reset or /new restart those totals, so the call total is the last result before each reset plus the final result.
why: Inside a query() call nothing but those three commands resets the running totals.
check: If a runner keeps one long streaming session and sends /clear between tasks, check that it adds the last pre-reset result to the final one; summing every result inflates cost.
quote: To total the whole call, add the last result from before each `/clear` to the call's final result. Every other result, including the `/clear` turn's own, is superseded by a later one.

claim: Agent SDK prompt-cache entries for main-conversation turns default to a 5-minute TTL with API-key authentication or on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry or Claude Platform on AWS.
why: With that TTL, short sessions using the same system prompt and context pay full input price after a gap longer than 5 minutes.
check: If repeated short sessions pay full input price, check the provider, authentication and time between runs before evaluating a longer TTL.
quote: Cache entries for your own turns use a 5-minute TTL by default when you authenticate with an API key or run on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry, or [Claude Platform on AWS](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-platform-on-aws.md).

claim: In single-message input mode Claude Code waits for background subagents still running at the end of the final turn before emitting the result, up to a cap, and the result's total_cost_usd and modelUsage include work done during that wait.
why: The result is emitted only after the wait, so wall time and cost can exceed the main loop's own.
check: Check runner timeouts and cost expectations for headless runs that start background subagents; the process may stay alive after the last assistant turn.
quote: Claude Code waits for background subagents still running at the end of the final turn before emitting the result.

claim: When systemPrompt is not set, the Agent SDK uses a minimal prompt that covers tool calling but omits the claude_code preset's security and safety instructions, unlike claude -p which uses the Claude Code system prompt by default.
why: The SDK default is deliberately a thin tool-calling loop; matching CLI behavior requires setting the claude_code preset.
check: If a runner migrates from claude -p and expects the same tool-use and safety guidance, check that it selects the claude_code preset instead of relying on the SDK default.
quote: the SDK uses a minimal prompt that covers tool calling but omits the rest of the `claude_code` preset's content, including its security and safety instructions. This differs from `claude -p`, which uses the Claude Code system prompt by default. If you're migrating from the CLI and want matching behavior, set the `claude_code` preset.

claim: Unattended coding automation such as a CI job that fixes lint errors or reviews diffs still fits the claude_code preset, while a custom prompt string suits non-coding agents or a different identity or permission model.
why: The preset is written for coding work, and a custom string replaces tool guidance and safety instructions that the agent must then supply itself.
check: If a headless code-review or fix runner replaces the preset with a custom string, check whether the replacement supplies the tool guidance and safety instructions the task needs.
quote: Unattended coding automation, like a CI job that fixes lint errors or reviews diffs, still fits the preset because the work itself is what the preset is written for.

claim: The SDK loads working-directory CLAUDE.md or .claude/CLAUDE.md through the project setting source and ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md through the user source, both of which default query() options enable.
why: Setting sources control whether the SDK loads these files regardless of the system prompt preset.
check: If a runner sets settingSources explicitly and relies on project or user CLAUDE.md, check that it includes the source for the file it needs.
quote: Default `query()` options enable both sources, so CLAUDE.md loads automatically. If you set `settingSources` in TypeScript or `setting_sources` in Python explicitly, include the sources you need. CLAUDE.md loading is controlled by setting sources, not by the `claude_code` preset.

claim: With the SDK's default system-prompt recording on, resume or continue reuses the recorded prompt until compaction, even if you pass a different append or custom prompt.
why: Claude Code records the prompt on the session's first request to keep the cached prefix stable, and changed prompt text can take effect in a new session.
check: For a runner that needs instructions on the next turn, check whether it sends them in a user message or via a hook's additionalContext and whether its SDK configuration records the prompt.
quote: By default, if you pass a different `append` or custom prompt when you return to a session with `resume` or `continue`, Claude doesn't see it on the next turn. Claude Code records the system prompt on a session's first request and reuses that record until the session is compacted. The new text takes effect after that compaction, or in a new session.

claim: A Python SDK system prompt passed as a string goes to the CLI subprocess as one command-line argument, so a prompt larger than the OS argument limit fails at process spawn before any API request; use system_prompt={"type": "file", "path": ...} for large prompts.
why: Operating systems cap argv length (on Linux the error is Argument list too long).
check: If a Python runner assembles a custom prompt that could exceed the operating system's argument-length limit, check that it loads the prompt from a file.
quote: The Python SDK passes a string prompt as one command-line argument to the CLI subprocess, so a prompt that exceeds the OS argument-length limit fails at process spawn before any API request is sent.

claim: Claude can still receive built-in commit guidance through the Bash tool description with a custom systemPrompt, so includeGitInstructions: false disables the built-in workflow instructions and empty attribution.commit and attribution.pr remove the Co-Authored-By trailer and pull request footer.
why: Claude would otherwise receive two conflicting instructions for the same commit.
check: If a runner replaces the default commit or pull request guidance, check whether built-in Git instructions and attribution still conflict with the format it wants.
quote: Set `includeGitInstructions` to `false` to keep out the built-in commit and pull request instructions, which are part of the Bash tool's description and reach Claude even with a custom `systemPrompt`.

claim: A custom systemPrompt string replaces the preset's explanation of system reminders, so without a sentence saying so, nothing tells Claude that CLAUDE.md content and hook output injected as reminders come from the application rather than the user.
why: Claude Code sends system reminders in the conversation, so most reach Claude with either the preset or a custom systemPrompt string.
check: If a runner uses a custom prompt string together with CLAUDE.md or hooks that add context, check the prompt includes a line explaining system reminders.
quote: If you pass your own string as `systemPrompt`, add a sentence to it that says what a system reminder is. The `claude_code` preset has one, and your string replaces the whole preset.

claim: The SDK message stream does not include system reminders, so reading received messages does not show what Claude saw; set OTEL_LOG_RAW_API_BODIES to file:<dir> or route ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL through a logging proxy to see the actual request bodies.
why: Reminders are added inside user messages in the request, outside the SDK stream.
check: When auditing or debugging what a headless run was given (CLAUDE.md, skills list, hook output), check request-body logging is available rather than inferring from stream messages.
quote: The SDK message stream doesn't include system reminders, so reading the messages your code receives won't show you what Claude saw.

claim: In the TypeScript SDK, passing env replaces the inherited subprocess environment, so spread process.env into it if the runner needs to retain inherited variables.
why: TypeScript env is a replacement, not a merge.
check: If a TypeScript runner sets options.env, check that it preserves or explicitly supplies the PATH, authentication and other variables its subprocess needs.
quote: In TypeScript, [`env`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/typescript#options) replaces the inherited environment, so spread `process.env` into it.

claim: To change instructions in a running or resumed SDK session, send them in the next user message or return additionalContext from a UserPromptSubmit or PostToolUse hook, rather than changing systemPrompt.
why: The SDK inserts hook text into the conversation at the point where the hook fired, leaving the recorded system prompt unchanged.
check: Check that a runner which edits systemPrompt between resumed turns to change mode (for example read-only) switches to a message or hook context instead.
quote: If the instructions you put in the system prompt need to change while a session is running, for example because your user switched the agent to a read-only mode or edited its configuration in your app, send the new instructions in the conversation instead of changing `systemPrompt`:

claim: Two SDK sessions using the same claude_code preset and append text cannot share a prompt cache entry by default when their auto memory locations differ, and excludeDynamicSections: true moves that context into the first user message, where Claude may follow auto-memory guidance less consistently.
why: CLAUDE.md and environment details like working directory, platform and OS do not affect the system prompt cache, but the auto memory location differs across users, machines and checkouts.
check: For a fleet sharing one task prompt with the claude_code preset, check whether differing auto memory paths hurt cache reuse and whether enabling excludeDynamicSections fits the fleet's needs.
quote: By default, two sessions that use the same `claude_code` preset and `append` text still can't share a prompt cache entry when their auto memory locations differ.

claim: The TypeScript SDK splits a custom prompt array at SYSTEM_PROMPT_DYNAMIC_BOUNDARY into separate cache blocks only on the direct Claude API or Claude Platform on AWS, and only if CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPERIMENTAL_BETAS is not set to 1.
why: Other configurations send the whole prompt as one block, so changing the per-request part also invalidates the static part of the cache.
check: Check that a runner expecting separate cache blocks puts the marker in its own array element between the static and per-request text and uses a supported configuration.
quote: Claude Code splits the prompt only when it calls the Claude API directly or runs on [Claude Platform on AWS]

claim: Omitting settingSources makes query() load the CLI's user, project and local filesystem inputs, including CLAUDE.md and .claude skills, agents and commands, while settingSources: [] skips those inputs.
why: The SDK uses the same filesystem settings as the CLI by default, and managed policy and global configuration are read regardless of settingSources.
check: Check that a runner wanting a clean, reproducible headless agent passes settingSources explicitly; relying on the default pulls in whatever the host's ~/.claude and the repo's .claude contain.
quote: When you omit `settingSources`, `query()` reads the same filesystem settings as the Claude Code CLI: user, project, and local settings, CLAUDE.md files, and `.claude/` skills, agents, and commands. To run without these, pass `settingSources: []`, which limits the agent to what you configure programmatically.

claim: settingSources: [] does not isolate an Agent SDK process from managed policy, ~/.claude.json, auto memory or MCP connectors loaded through a claude.ai login.
why: The SDK can pick up those inputs from the host or session independently of settingSources.
check: For a multi-tenant runner using settingSources: [], check which policy, global configuration and memory remain visible and whether the session's login loads connectors.
quote: Because the inputs above are read regardless of `settingSources`, an SDK process can pick up host-level configuration and per-directory memory.

claim: claude.ai MCP connectors load in an SDK session authenticated with a claude.ai login, are not loaded when CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN holds a setup-token token, and are not suppressed by mcpServers: {}; strictMcpConfig, disableClaudeAiConnectors or ENABLE_CLAUDEAI_MCP_SERVERS=false turn them off.
why: The connectors come from the account login rather than from the options the code passes.
check: If a runner authenticates with a claude.ai login and needs to exclude account connectors, check that it uses one of the connector controls instead of relying on mcpServers: {}.
quote: Loaded when the session authenticates with your claude.ai login. Not loaded when `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` holds a token from [`claude setup-token`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/authentication#generate-a-long-lived-token), which can only make model requests. Passing `mcpServers: {}` does not suppress the connectors

claim: With the project setting source enabled, the SDK looks under <cwd>/.claude/ for project settings.json and hooks without a parent-directory fallback, while project CLAUDE.md and rules load from cwd and its parent directories.
why: Different project inputs use different lookup rules relative to cwd.
check: If a runner starts in a subdirectory or worktree and needs the repository's project settings.json or hooks, check that its cwd and enabled setting sources make those files visible.
quote: `<cwd>/.claude/` for `settings.json` and hooks; `<cwd>` and every parent directory for CLAUDE.md and rules;

claim: In the SDK, discovered user and project skills are enabled by default and the Skill tool is available; the skills option takes "all", a list of names or [] to restrict, and if a tools list is also passed it must include "Skill" for Claude to invoke skills.
why: Skills are discovered through settingSources and gated by the tool list.
check: Check that a runner expecting skill invocation includes Skill in any explicit tool list, and use skills: [] to disable all discovered skills for the main agent.
quote: When the `skills` option on `query()` is omitted, discovered user and project skills are enabled and the Skill tool is available, matching CLI behavior. To control which skills the main agent can invoke, pass `skills` as `"all"`, a list of skill names, or `[]` to disable all. If you also pass a `tools` list, include `"Skill"` so Claude can invoke skills.

claim: The Agent SDK runs settings.json hooks loaded through settingSources alongside callbacks passed to query(), and both kinds of hook fire inside subagents.
why: Programmatic hooks receive agent_id and agent_type so a callback can identify the agent that fired it.
check: If a runner combines filesystem and programmatic hooks, check whether its audit accounts for both kinds firing in subagents.
quote:
These fire in the main agent and any subagents it spawns. |
| **Programmatic** (callbacks in `query()`) | Application-specific logic, structured decisions, and in-process integration. These also fire inside subagents.

claim: The SDK spend cap refuses new subagents with Budget limit reached, stops background subagents still running and ends the query with error_max_budget_usd, as documented for TypeScript SDK v0.3.219 and Python SDK v0.2.127 and later, which bundle Claude Code v2.1.219 or later.
why: Each subagent makes its own API requests that count toward total_cost_usd, and a subagent can spawn more subagents, so one prompt can grow into a tree.
check: Check the bundled Claude Code version when a runner relies on the spend cap to refuse new subagents and stop ones still running, since older SDK releases may lack some limits or use different defaults.
quote: Enforces the cap in three ways: refuses to spawn more subagents, returning `Budget limit reached`, stops background subagents that are still running, and ends the query with the `error_max_budget_usd` result subtype.

claim: An SDK subagent spawned by the main agent runs in the background by default and returns status async_launched with its report arriving in a later turn, while a blocking Agent call returns status completed when Claude waits for the report, which the prompt can ask it to do.
why: The default is non-blocking so the parent can continue working.
check: If the parent's answer needs to use a subagent's report, check that the workflow waits for the report before composing the answer.
quote:
By default, a subagent your main agent spawns [runs in the background](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents.md#run-subagents-in-foreground-or-background). The Agent tool result has `status: "async_launched"`, and the report arrives in a later turn.

Claude waits when its next action needs the report: the call blocks and returns `status: "completed"`.

claim: AgentDefinition.tools lists the tools a subagent may use but does not pre-approve them, and omitting tools gives the subagent every tool available to subagents; programmatically defined agents override filesystem agents with the same name.
why: Tool availability and approval are separate, so a read-only reviewer needs an appropriate available toolset even when approval is handled elsewhere.
check: Check whether a read-only reviewer restricts or removes tools that could change state, especially when omitting tools would inherit them from the available subagent toolset.
quote: Array of allowed tool names; listing one doesn't [pre-approve](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/permissions.md#allow-and-deny-rules) it. If omitted, inherits every [tool available to subagents]

claim: From Claude Code 2.1.302 Claude can start fork subagents in an SDK application with nothing configured by calling the Agent tool with subagent_type fork; an Agent(fork) deny rule in disallowedTools stops forks while other subagents still run.
why: A fork copies the conversation so far instead of starting fresh.
check: If a runner needs to prevent subagents from inheriting the parent's conversation through a fork, check whether it denies Agent(fork).
quote: From Claude Code v2.1.302, Claude can start forks in your application with nothing configured, by calling the Agent tool with `subagent_type: "fork"`.

claim: To resume an SDK subagent, resume its parent session using session_id and put the Agent result's agentId in the prompt, passing the same agent definition in both queries for a custom agent.
why: Each query() starts a new session by default, and the subagent transcript belongs to its original session.
check: Check that a runner saves both IDs, puts agentId in the follow-up prompt and reuses the definition for a custom agent.
quote:
pass `resume: sessionId` in the second query's options, and include the agent ID in your prompt. Each `query()` call starts a new session by default, and you must resume the same session to access the subagent's transcript.

> [!NOTE]
>
> When using a custom agent, pass the same agent definition in the `agents` parameter for both queries.

claim: With the Agent tool available, Claude can spawn the built-in general-purpose subagent even when no agents are defined, and CLAUDE_AGENT_SDK_DISABLE_BUILTIN_AGENTS=1 removes that default so a call without subagent_type fails with subagent_type is required.
why: The Agent tool uses the built-in general-purpose subagent by default when a call omits subagent_type.
check: For a locked-down headless run, check whether the Agent tool is left available without intent; a runner that wants no delegation should deny Agent rather than rely on defining no agents.
quote: it gets the built-in `general-purpose` subagent, which Claude can spawn even when you define no agents of your own.

claim: The subagent tool appears as Agent in tool_use blocks but as Task in the system:init tools list, and tool_use blocks used Task before Claude Code v2.1.63, so detectors spanning SDK versions should match both names.
why: The tool was renamed from Task to Agent.
check: If a log parser counts subagent invocations across Claude Code versions, check that it matches both Agent and Task in tool_use blocks.
quote: The tool appears as `"Agent"` in `tool_use` blocks but as `"Task"` in the `system:init` tools list. Before Claude Code v2.1.63, `tool_use` blocks also named it `"Task"`. To keep detection working across SDK versions, match both values in `block.name`.

claim: Since Claude Code v2.1.210, the scan of a subagent's final message escapes harness-only tags after the opening angle bracket and line-start Human: or Assistant: markers before the colon.
why: Claude Code adds escapes before the parent reads the message and never removes or rewords the subagent's text.
check: If a pipeline parses a subagent's final message, check whether it tolerates the inserted backslashes.
quote: Claude Code neutralizes a tag that only the harness emits, such as a `<system-reminder>` block, in place. It inserts a backslash after the opening angle bracket and deletes nothing.

claim: Claude Opus 5 delegates to subagents more readily than earlier models.
why: Claude Code enforces depth, concurrency and spend limits regardless of how Claude decides to delegate.
check: For an Opus 5 runner, check whether the depth, concurrency and spend limits meet the run's needs.
quote: Claude Opus 5 delegates to subagents more readily than earlier models, so the [depth, concurrency, and spend limits](#cap-subagent-depth-concurrency-and-spend) matter most on queries that run Opus 5.

claim: For most Agent SDK hook events, a callback that throws, returns invalid output or returns nothing triggers a hook_callback_failed warning and lets the action proceed by default.
why: A failed PreToolUse guard leaves the call to the normal permission flow.
check: Check whether a runner detects hook_callback_failed and whether a guard that must stop the action relies on the default failure behavior.
quote: On most events, if a callback throws or returns output that fails validation, the action goes ahead and your app receives an [`SDKInformationalMessage`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/typescript#sdkinformationalmessage) warning whose `tag` is `hook_callback_failed`.

claim: With onFailure block, the Stop, SubagentStop, TaskCompleted and TeammateIdle events ignore the option and the action goes ahead, PermissionRequest blocks only if the block arrives before canUseTool answers, and PostToolUse can only report the failure since the tool already ran.
why: A callback failure only reports feedback after PostToolUse, and a PermissionRequest failure can block only before the permission callback answers.
check: If a runner relies on a Stop or SubagentStop callback as a quality gate, check that a crash or timeout of that callback is not assumed to hold the agent back.
quote: **`Stop`, `SubagentStop`, `TaskCompleted`, and `TeammateIdle`**: these events ignore the option, so the action goes ahead.

claim: The SDK cancels a timed-out hook callback and discards its output, blocking the tool call for PreToolUse and the prompt for UserPromptSubmit while keeping the session alive.
why: Unlike SDK callbacks, the documented defaults for command hooks let a timed-out PreToolUse decision fall through unless onFailure is block and let a timed-out UserPromptSubmit prompt through.
check: When auditing timeouts, check whether the hook is an SDK callback or a command hook before assuming whether a timeout fails open or closed.
quote: `PreToolUse`: Claude Code blocks the tool call. If every other hook returned nothing or only an `allow` decision, the tool result tells Claude the hook didn't respond before its timeout, and the turn continues.

claim: Before Claude Code 2.1.210 a timed-out PreToolUse callback was reported to Claude as a user rejection, which made unattended sessions stop and wait for input; before 2.1.208 a timed-out UserPromptSubmit or UserPromptExpansion callback ended the query with error_during_execution.
why: Older versions treated hook timeouts as user actions or fatal errors.
check: For a runner pinned to a Claude Code older than 2.1.210 that uses PreToolUse callbacks, check for hung unattended sessions after slow hooks.
quote: Before v2.1.210, Claude Code reported the timeout to Claude as a user rejection, which made unattended sessions stop and wait for input.

claim: SDK hook callback timeouts default to the event's timeout, 600 seconds for most events, 30 seconds for UserPromptSubmit, PreModelSwitch and PostModelSwitch, and 10 seconds for MessageDisplay, with SessionEnd callbacks running under a shutdown timeout budget of 1.5 seconds by default.
why: Work in a SessionEnd callback has to fit within the active shutdown budget.
check: Check whether a SessionEnd callback doing network or disk work can finish within the configured shutdown timeout.
quote: When you don't set one, Claude Code uses the event's default: 600 seconds for most events, 30 seconds for `UserPromptSubmit`, `PreModelSwitch`, and `PostModelSwitch`, and 10 seconds for `MessageDisplay`. Claude Code runs `SessionEnd` callbacks during shutdown under the shorter [SessionEnd timeout budget](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks.md#sessionend-input), 1.5 seconds by default.

claim: Hooks may not fire when the agent hits the max_turns limit because the session ends before hooks can execute.
why: A session can reach its turn limit and end before a hook executes.
check: If a runner relies on a Stop or SessionEnd hook to record results, check it also records from the result message so a max-turns exit is not lost.
quote: Hooks may not fire when the agent hits the [`max_turns`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/python#claudeagentoptions) limit because the session ends before hooks can execute

claim: Hook matchers match only the event's target such as the tool name, not file paths or arguments, so a Write|Edit matcher guarding .env does not run when Claude writes the file through Bash, and a file-path check written with forward slashes misses Windows backslash paths such as C:\project\.env.
why: Filtering by path has to be done inside the callback, and Bash writes need the sandbox or a Bash matcher.
check: For a hook protecting a file, check coverage for shell writes and whether its path comparisons account for backslashes on Windows.
quote: If Claude writes `.env` with a Bash command, the hook doesn't run.

claim: Matching hooks for one event run in parallel with non-deterministic completion order, and for competing PreToolUse permission decisions the most restrictive wins in the order deny, defer, ask, then allow.
why: Hooks must therefore act independently rather than rely on another hook having run first.
check: Check that a setup does not depend on hook ordering, for example one hook rewriting input for another; and that an allow hook cannot override another hook's deny.
quote: When multiple `PreToolUse` hooks return different [decisions](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks.md#pretooluse-decision-control), `deny` takes priority over `defer`, which takes priority over `ask`, which takes priority over `allow`.

claim: A PreToolUse hook returning permissionDecision defer ends the turn with a result whose stop_reason is tool_deferred so the call can be resumed later, which gives an unattended runner a way to hold a sensitive call for later approval instead of denying it.
why: Defer pauses the call rather than allowing or denying it, and updatedInput is ignored when deferring.
check: If a headless runner defers tool calls for a later decision, check that it handles tool_deferred and can resume the pending call.
quote: If you return `"defer"`, the turn ends with a result message whose `stop_reason` is `"tool_deferred"`, so you can [resume the call later]

claim: Non-interactive claude -p --worktree skips the workspace trust check and has no exit prompt, so Claude Code leaves the worktree on disk and leaves its creation lock for a later stale-lock sweep to release, and git worktree remove may require git worktree unlock first.
why: Cleanup decisions are made by an interactive exit prompt that -p does not have.
check: If a runner creates disposable worktrees with -p --worktree, check how it removes them after the run and handles a creation lock that remains.
quote: Non-interactive runs with `-p` have no exit prompt, so Claude doesn't clean up their worktrees, and Claude Code leaves the lock it took on each one at creation in place until a later session's [stale-lock sweep]

claim: With the default worktree.baseRef of "fresh", a new worktree branches from the remote's default branch unless no remote is configured or origin/HEAD is unavailable, while "head" uses local HEAD and a --worktree pull request reference fetches that request's head commit.
why: A fresh worktree is meant to match the remote and start from a clean tree.
check: If a worktree session needs in-progress local commits, check whether it is created from local HEAD rather than relying on the default remote base.
quote: If no remote is configured, or `origin/HEAD` isn't cached locally and can't be fetched, the worktree falls back to your current local `HEAD`.

claim: Worktree isolation checks file-edit targets and, for Bash and Monitor, command directories and git use, while PowerShell receives only the directory check and shell writes into the main checkout without running git there remain subject to ordinary permissions and sandboxing.
why: The four checks cover file-edit tools, command working directory, git redirects and command shape only.
check: Where worktrees are the isolation boundary for parallel or unattended sessions, check that sandboxing or deny rules also cover shell writes to the main checkout.
quote: None of them tracks which files a shell command writes, so a command that writes into the main checkout without running git there, such as `cp` or a shell redirect, isn't refused by them.

claim: In -p mode and for Agent SDK resumes, a refused worktree resume stops with a stderr error except when the worktree is gone, and with stream-json the refusal also produces error_during_execution from v2.1.260 with startup_failure_reason worktree_unverified or worktree_resume_refused from v2.1.274.
why: The non-interactive refusal stops that resume without re-entering the worktree, while a gone worktree leaves the session to continue in the launch directory.
check: Check that a runner resuming worktree-bound sessions handles both a refused resume and the notice that a deleted worktree caused resume in the launch directory.
quote: In [non-interactive mode](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless.md) with `-p`, and on resumes that the [Agent SDK](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/sessions.md) runs, Claude Code stops the resume with a stderr error for every refusal except a gone worktree, instead of continuing without isolation.

claim: Resuming a session that ended isolated in a worktree re-enters that worktree if it verifies (including non-interactive and SDK resumes from v2.1.212), while --fork-session starts in the launch directory and --continue selects the most recent session recorded there.
why: The worktree binding belongs to the original session, not to the fork.
check: If a fork of a worktree-bound session must operate on the worktree's files, check where it is launched.
quote: **`--fork-session`**: the forked session starts in the directory you launched Claude from, and Claude Code leaves the original session's worktree untouched.

claim: A reused --worktree resets to the default branch only with a fresh base, a name other than a PR/MR reference, unrestricted sandbox writes, sandbox off in both checkouts, and a verifiably clean worktree on its original branch with no commits of its own or with a merged PR/MR whose remote branch was deleted.
why: Claude Code keeps the old tip whenever a reset condition fails or it cannot verify the worktree state.
check: If a runner reuses names across runs, check the actual branch and tip before assuming it started from the default branch.
quote:
* The [sandbox](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing.md#filesystem-isolation) isn't restricting file writes in your session, and neither the worktree's nor the main checkout's `.claude` settings files enable the sandbox.
* The worktree has no uncommitted changes or untracked files.
* It is still on the branch Claude Code created for it.

claim: Outside Windows, when Claude Code uses the repository root for approvals, choosing "Yes, and don't ask again" for Bash in a worktree saves the rule to the main checkout's .claude/settings.local.json.
why: That local rule applies in the main checkout and every worktree of the repository, and it survives removal of the worktree.
check: Check the main checkout for approval rules from removed worktrees and check the worktree itself on Windows or whenever the repository root is unused.
quote: choosing "Yes, and don't ask again" for a Bash command in a worktree session saves the rule to the main checkout's `.claude/settings.local.json`. The rule applies in the main checkout and in every other worktree of the repository, and it survives the worktree's removal.

claim: After Claude enters a worktree, ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR} in hook commands still points at the starting project root, so a script referenced under that path still comes from the main checkout, while the cwd field in the hook input JSON follows Claude into the worktree and changes again on cd.
why: Claude Code keeps the hook path stable and passes the worktree path through the input JSON.
check: Check worktree-based setups for hooks that use ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR} to find files being edited; they should read cwd from the hook input.
quote: it still points at the project root where the session started, so a hook command such as `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/.claude/hooks/check-style.sh` still runs the script in the main checkout.

claim: A new worktree is a fresh checkout without gitignored files such as .env; a .worktreeinclude file at the project root in .gitignore syntax copies matching gitignored files into every worktree Claude Code creates with git, but it is not processed when a WorktreeCreate hook replaces creation.
why: Only files that match a pattern and are also gitignored are copied.
check: If a headless worktree run needs ignored files from the main checkout, check that they are available in the new worktree through .worktreeinclude for git-based creation or through the WorktreeCreate hook when it creates the worktree.
quote: Only files that match a pattern and are also gitignored are copied, so tracked files are never duplicated.

claim: Since Claude Code v2.1.247, a worktree it creates contains Git LFS pointer files when LFS was set up with git lfs install --local because Claude Code skips repository-configured filter drivers, and git lfs pull inside the worktree retrieves the content.
why: A filter driver is a shell command that anything able to write to the repository could have planted.
check: If tests or review in a worktree need LFS content and LFS is configured locally in the repository, check that the checkout holds the real files instead of pointers.
quote: a worktree that Claude Code creates contains LFS pointer files instead of the real files.

claim: A subagent running in its own worktree takes its starting instruction files from the main conversation, and when the worktree is under .claude/worktrees it does not load the worktree root's CLAUDE.md or .claude/rules as it reads files there, even if they differ on the worktree's branch.
why: The subagent's instruction context is built from the parent session, not the worktree.
check: If a reviewer needs branch-specific CLAUDE.md or rules in a worktree under .claude/worktrees, check how it receives those instructions given that the worktree-root copies are not loaded automatically.
quote: the subagent also doesn't load the `CLAUDE.md` file or `.claude/rules/` directory at the worktree's root as it reads files there, even if those differ on the worktree's branch.

claim: A routine treats text from /fire or Run now as inert context unless its saved prompt explicitly tells Claude to act on the <routine-fire-payload> block.
why: The wrapper labels the text as untrusted because anyone holding the bearer token can submit fire text.
check: For a routine that acts on submitted alerts, check that its saved prompt explicitly directs Claude to investigate the alert in the routine-fire-payload block.
quote: This means a routine's saved prompt must opt in to acting on fire text: write the prompt to reference the payload explicitly, for example "Investigate the alert described in the routine-fire-payload block", or the routine treats the text as inert context.

claim: A routine's saved prompt is carried out as its assignment but is not live user input and cannot act as approval or consent for actions during the run; content fetched during the run keeps its normal handling.
why: The trigger attests only that an authorized session on the account stored the prompt ahead of time.
check: Check that a routine whose prompt says "you are authorized to delete/push/merge" does not rely on that sentence to get approval for gated actions.
quote: The fired prompt is therefore not live user input and can't act as approval or consent for actions during the run.

claim: A routine run starting a new cloud session begins in auto mode unless auto mode is unavailable, and it still stops and waits for a human when an action matches an ask rule or when blocks reach auto mode's repeated-block thresholds, so an unattended routine can stall on a prompt nobody sees.
why: Auto mode lets a classifier allow or block actions, but ask rules and repeated blocks fall back to a permission prompt in the run's session.
check: For an unattended cloud routine in auto mode, check whether needed actions still require approval and how someone will find and answer a waiting prompt when they do.
quote: When a run starts a new session on Anthropic's cloud, that session begins in [auto mode](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes.md#eliminate-prompts-with-auto-mode) unless auto mode is unavailable. In auto mode, a classifier model allows or blocks actions that would otherwise wait for your approval.

claim: A routine includes the account's connected MCP connectors by default, with their write tools, while a server added only with local claude mcp add must be added as a connector or declared in a committed .mcp.json for a single-repository task that does not run as project threads.
why: Connectors belong to the claude.ai account while local MCP servers live on the machine.
check: Check a routine's connector list for unnecessary access and verify that a server it needs is available as a connector or through a supported repository declaration.
quote: Remove any the task doesn't need: Claude can use an included connector during a run, including writes.

claim: Run now, API fires and reruns of one-off tasks share a cap of 30 starts per scheduled task per hour, with further attempts failing until the cap resets.
why: Scheduled tasks have hourly caps that do not allow overage.
check: If a task has multiple ways to start, check that the runner counts all three against the same per-task limit.
quote: | **Run now**, API fires, and setting a one-off task to run again | 30 per hour | Each scheduled task, one count shared by all three | The action fails until the limit resets |

claim: In a routine's history, Succeeded means only that the session ended without Claude Code reporting a failure, so blocked network requests, missing connector tools and work Claude could not complete appear only in the transcript, not on the row.
why: The status describes how the session ended, not whether the prompt's work was done.
check: Check that anyone relying on routine status for monitoring also reads transcripts or has the routine report its own outcome; a green row does not prove the task completed.
quote: the session ended without Claude Code reporting a failure. Blocked network requests, missing connector tools, and work Claude couldn't complete appear in the transcript rather than on the row

claim: Routines belong solely to the creating claude.ai account, actions through linked GitHub or connector accounts appear as that owner, and self-hosted runs can push with deployment-provided Git credentials.
why: GitHub applies branch rules to the connected GitHub access for Anthropic-managed runs and self-hosted runs using Anthropic's Git proxy, or to deployment credentials when the run pushes with those credentials.
check: Check whether a routine's ownership and the GitHub and connector identities attributed to its actions match the team's requirements.
quote: Scheduled tasks belong to your individual claude.ai account. They are not shared with teammates

claim: A cross-session message carries plain text without attaching the sender's history or files, cannot approve a permission prompt or execute a slash command, and comes with an instruction for the receiver to leave configuration unchanged while its own permission rules and prompts still apply.
why: Permission boundaries stay per-session, and a message never counts as the user's consent.
check: If one session steers another, check that the workflow obtains approvals and configuration changes through the receiving session's own controls instead of asking for them by message.
quote: **It can't approve anything**: a message from another session never counts as your consent, so it can't answer a pending permission prompt on your behalf.

claim: With no crossSessionInbound value set, a session that prompts for permissions accepts messages (holding only those from a sender that bypasses prompts), whereas a session running with bypassed permission prompts holds each incoming message for human approval unless the sender also bypasses.
why: The inbound default evaluates the sender and receiver's permission-mode classes for each message.
check: If a bypassing receiver must accept messages unattended from a sender that does not bypass prompts, check the effective crossSessionInbound setting because the default holds those messages.
quote: **The receiving session bypasses permission prompts**: Claude Code holds each message for your approval. It delivers one only when the sending session identifies itself as also bypassing.

claim: In a messaging-enabled claude -p session, a message held by the inbound default expires at dialogExpiry (five minutes by default) unless accepted first or dialogExpiry is set to never.
why: A -p session cannot show the approval dialog, and setting dialogExpiry to never holds these messages until the session ends unless they are accepted.
check: For an unattended worker with the default inbound rule, check whether messages held for approval can expire before an applicable mode or settings change accepts them.
quote:
When the [inbound default](#control-inbound-messages) holds a message there, Claude Code keeps it for the same [`dialogExpiry`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#dialogexpiry) deadline the dialog uses, five minutes by default:

* **Before the deadline**: if a mode or settings change allows the message, Claude Code delivers it.

claim: Each delivered cross-session message counts toward usage like a typed prompt, and two sessions on the same machine that answer slowly enough to avoid throttling can exchange thousands of messages without a prompt from the user.
why: Throttling does not necessarily stop slow reply loops, though long exchanges can pause sending and some reply chains can be cut off.
check: Where autonomous sessions can keep replying to each other, check whether the workflow limits the exchange and can stop it by ending a session or refusing inbound messages.
quote: two sessions that answer each other slowly enough not to be throttled can exchange thousands of messages without a prompt from you, and each delivered message [counts toward usage](#message-delivery).

claim: The platform minimum for cross-session messaging is Claude Code v2.1.224 on macOS, Linux and WSL 2, and v2.1.234 on native Windows.
why: Provider and feature-flag configuration can impose an additional version requirement for same-machine messaging.
check: If /list-agents is unavailable, check claude --version against the platform minimum and any provider-specific requirement.
quote: Cross-session messaging requires Claude Code v2.1.224 or later on macOS, Linux, and WSL 2, and v2.1.234 or later on native Windows.

claim: Denying SendMessage and ListAgents in permissions stops a session from sending and listing, but SendMessage is the same tool used for subagents and agent-team teammates, so denying it also removes messaging to them; crossSessionInbound refuse separately drops inbound messages.
why: Sending and receiving are separate controls, and the tool serves both peer and in-session messaging.
check: Before adding a SendMessage deny rule to a setup that uses subagents or agent teams, check it will not break their coordination.
quote: Denying `SendMessage` also removes messaging to subagents and agent-team teammates, since the same tool serves both.

claim: When cross-session messaging is enabled and an inbox binds, Claude Code exports CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_SOCKET and CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_TOKEN to hooks and Bash commands for posting to their own session.
why: The variables identify the session's inbox and supply its per-session authentication token.
check: If a hook posts to its own session, check whether the messaging inbox bound and whether the hook receives the socket and token from its own process environment.
quote: Alongside the socket's path, Claude Code exports a per-session token as [`CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_TOKEN`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars#variables). A script posting to its own session's socket can send `{"type":"auth","token":"<token>"}` as the first line of its connection, where `<token>` is the value of `CLAUDE_CODE_MESSAGING_TOKEN`.

claim: Claude Code rejects claude --bg combined with -p or --print before creating a session because print mode does not start the supervisor-hosted interactive session that claude agents attaches to.
why: Background sessions are interactive sessions hosted by a supervisor, not print-mode runs.
check: If a runner script builds claude -p --bg commands, check that it picks one mode; the combination fails at launch.
quote: Claude Code rejects `--bg` combined with `-p` or `--print` before any session is created, because `--print` never starts the interactive session that `claude agents` attaches to.

claim: With claude --bg, an unknown --agent name triggers a no agent named warning and an immediate --agent not found exit, even though Claude Code reports the session as backgrounded.
why: The backgrounded message can appear before the session rejects the agent name.
check: If a runner dispatches with --bg --agent, check for an immediate exit using claude agents --json instead of treating the backgrounded line as success.
quote: If the name doesn't match any of your subagents, the launch fails: Claude Code prints a `no agent named` warning and still reports the session as backgrounded, but the session exits immediately with an `--agent '<name>' not found` error.

claim: By default, a session dispatched from agent view or started with claude --bg moves into an isolated worktree before editing files in its working directory.
why: The launch starts in the working directory and Claude moves the session before the edit.
check: For parallel background edits, check that isolation actually applies to each session and target file.
quote: Before editing files, Claude moves the session into an isolated [git worktree](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/worktrees.md) under `.claude/worktrees/`, so parallel sessions can read the same checkout but each writes to its own.

claim: When a background session changes code in a worktree Claude entered, Claude Code tells it to commit without asking and push the branch if there is a remote, unless the task, CLAUDE.md or memory leaves those actions to you.
why: Claude Code instructs the agent to preserve the work before the session and its worktree can be deleted.
check: If the user must retain control of committing or pushing, check whether the task, CLAUDE.md or memory says so.
quote: **Commit and push**: Claude commits without asking, and pushes the branch when the repository has a remote.

claim: Deleting a background session in agent view removes its Claude-created worktree and uncommitted edits if the worktree still has its .git file and has no unpushed commits.
why: Agent view can remove dirty worktrees, while some worktree directories stay on disk when their .git file is gone.
check: Before deleting a session in agent view, check its worktree for uncommitted changes that need to be kept.
quote: Agent view removes it, including uncommitted changes, so commit what you want to keep first.

claim: The supported way to poll background sessions from a script is claude agents --json --all, which keeps listing sessions after their processes exit.
why: The files under ~/.claude/jobs/<id>/ are an unstable interface, and --all keeps exited sessions visible.
check: Check that completion polling uses the supported command and keeps exited sessions visible instead of parsing state.json.
quote: `claude agents --json` is the supported way to read session state from outside Claude Code, for example from a status bar, a scheduler, or another Claude session that supervises background work. Poll `claude agents --json --all`, which keeps listing sessions whose process has exited, and read each entry's `state`, `status`, and `waitingFor`.

claim: A background session with state blocked needs user input or action before continuing, and the supervisor keeps its process running while it is paused on an open permission prompt or other dialog.
why: blocked always means the session needs something from the user before it continues.
check: If a runner polls unattended background sessions, check that it surfaces state blocked and reads waitingFor when present to identify what needs attention.
quote: `blocked` | The session is waiting on you: a question it asked, a permission or sandbox decision, an error only you can clear such as an expired login, or its first prompt if you started it without one. When the wait is an open prompt in a live process, `waitingFor` names it

claim: For dispatch from an agent view opened with the left-arrow key, Claude Code rejects a defaultMode in the project's .claude/settings.json or .claude/settings.local.json if it is more permissive than the originating session's mode.
why: Claude Code tries the next source when it rejects a mode as too permissive.
check: Check the originating session's mode and which project file sets defaultMode before relying on a more permissive mode for the dispatched session.
quote: Claude Code refuses a `defaultMode` from the project's `.claude/settings.json` or `.claude/settings.local.json` that selects a more permissive mode than the session you came from was in.

claim: Moving a Claude Code session to the background preserves --mcp-config, --strict-mcp-config, --settings, --setting-sources, --add-dir, --plugin-dir, --fallback-model and --allow-dangerously-skip-permissions.
why: The backgrounded session carries the listed configuration flags from its original launch.
check: If a moved session relies on strict MCP or custom setting sources, check the flags on its original launch.
quote:
Configuration flags from the original launch carry through to the backgrounded session, so its MCP servers, settings, and fallback model remain in effect:

* `--mcp-config` and `--strict-mcp-config`
* `--settings`
* `--setting-sources`
* `--add-dir`
* `--plugin-dir`
* `--fallback-model`
* `--allow-dangerously-skip-permissions`

claim: A shell-only gateway ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL reaches a background session only if the supervisor started with the same exported gateway and you either background your own session (← or /background) or dispatch, wake or respawn one from its own directory.
why: Gateway values in a settings file's env block are read with the rest of the background session's settings.
check: Check whether gateway variables are in the applicable settings env block when a background runner needs the gateway across dispatch, wake or restart from another directory.
quote:
* You background your own session with `←` or `/background`
* You dispatch a session into the directory you're in
* You wake a stopped session in the directory you're in by attaching or replying to it
* You restart a session in the directory you're in with [`claude respawn`](#manage-sessions-from-the-shell)

claim: The supervisor stops an unpinned background process when its session has been unattached for about an hour and either has finished or is waiting for the next message.
why: The conversation stays on disk and resumes on attach or reply.
check: If an idle session must keep its process running, check whether it is pinned and whether the runner handles resuming an unpinned session.
quote: * **Finished or waiting for your next message, and unattached for about an hour**: the supervisor stops the process to free resources. A session that ended its turn by asking you a question counts as waiting for your next message. The conversation stays on disk, and the next time you attach or reply, the session resumes where it left off. Pin a session with `Ctrl+T` to keep its process running.

claim: After a machine shutdown, agent view keeps background sessions awaiting your input under Needs input and marks other previously running sessions as failed within 48 hours of their last progress or stopped after that.
why: Machine shutdown stops running background processes, and their saved conversations can remain available on disk.
check: Check whether recovery distinguishes Needs input, failed and stopped sessions and can resume the saved conversation when it still exists.
quote:
For any other running session, what agent view shows depends on how long ago it last made progress:

* Within 48 hours, the session shows as failed. Attach or reply to it and it restarts from its saved conversation. To pick the interrupted work back up, send it a reply asking it to continue.
* Past 48 hours, such as after the machine was off for days, the session shows as stopped

claim: claude --bg --exec runs a shell command as a PTY job with no model, its output is held in memory only, and the row and output are cleaned up about five minutes after the command exits, so a script must read it within that window.
why: Shell job output is not written to disk.
check: If a runner needs output from a --bg --exec job, check that it reads claude logs or captures the output before the row and output are cleaned up about five minutes after exit.
quote: The captured output stays in memory and isn't written to disk. The row and its output clean up automatically about five minutes after the command exits

claim: claude --resume <full-session-id> --bg continues the session under the same ID on 2.1.257+ or starts a copy under a new ID with a note, while combining --bg with --continue, a bare --resume, or --resume by name or path always starts a copy.
why: Only a full session ID can be continued in place.
check: If a runner resumes background work by name, check that it expects a new session ID and updates its bookkeeping.
quote: When you combine `--bg` with `--continue`, a bare `--resume`, or `--resume` with a name or file path, Claude Code always starts such a copy.

claim: Agent view refuses to fork a session started with launch flags the copy would not inherit, such as a replaced system prompt or --tools allowlist, and its dispatch input rejects prompts shorter than four characters.
why: Claude Code refuses rather than making a partial copy.
check: If a reviewer flow forks a runner session started with --system-prompt or --tools, check it expects the fork to be refused.
quote: Sessions started with launch flags the copy wouldn't inherit, such as a replaced system prompt or a `--tools` allowlist, can't be forked

claim: A Claude Code session dispatched from an agent view opened with the left-arrow key can fall back from inherited bypassPermissions to Manual if disclaimer acceptance is recorded only in .claude/settings.local.json or a --settings file.
why: The inherited bypassPermissions mode depends on where acceptance of the bypass disclaimer is stored.
check: If a dispatch reports that bypass permissions were ignored, check whether the disclaimer acceptance is recorded in ~/.claude/settings.json and inspect the effective mode.
quote: If that session was in `bypassPermissions` mode, the new session can start in Manual mode instead, with the notice `Bypass permissions was requested at launch and ignored`. That happens when your acceptance of the bypass disclaimer is only in `.claude/settings.local.json` or a `--settings` file.

claim: --allowedTools lets matching tools run without prompting for permission, except for reads from network paths.
why: The flag grants permission for matching calls and leaves tool availability to other controls.
check: If a headless runner uses --allowedTools to build a closed toolset, check which tools are actually available separately from which ones can run without prompting.
quote: Tools that execute without prompting for permission, apart from reads from [network paths](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions.md#network-paths).

claim: --tools restricts Claude Code's built-in tools and leaves MCP tools unaffected.
why: MCP tools are outside the built-in tool set controlled by this flag.
check: If a headless run needs a closed toolset, check the built-ins in --tools and use --disallowedTools for unwanted MCP tools.
quote: The flag doesn't affect MCP tools; to deny those too, use `--disallowedTools "mcp__*"`.

claim: In a non-interactive run with --permission-prompt-tool, Claude Code waits before the first turn for that tool's MCP server to connect, up to MCP_TIMEOUT (30 seconds by default).
why: The permission prompt handler is a tool on an MCP server loaded by the non-interactive run.
check: Check that the runner loads the named MCP tool and gives its server time to connect before the first turn.
quote: Claude Code waits for that tool's MCP server to connect before running the first turn, up to the [`MCP_TIMEOUT`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars) startup timeout, 30 seconds by default.

claim: ENABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_1H requests a 1-hour TTL for both Agent SDK cache buckets, and CLAUDE_CODE_PROMPT_CACHE_TTL and CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_PROMPT_CACHE_TTL override it for the main conversation and all other requests, respectively.
why: A longer TTL trades more expensive cache writes for more opportunities to read from the cache.
check: Check the effective TTL for each bucket when a runner enables 1-hour caching, since the per-bucket overrides take precedence.
