quote: `ENABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_1H` asks for the 1-hour TTL on every request in both buckets. To choose a TTL for each bucket separately, use these controls instead. Each takes `5m` or `1h` and takes precedence over `ENABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_1H`:

claim: With SDK prompt recording off, a changed append or custom prompt on resume reaches Claude on the next turn at the cost of a prompt cache miss and, where the API enforces preserved thinking, loss of earlier thinking.
why: Setting snapshot to false on the object form rebuilds the system prompt on every request.
check: Check whether a production runner has disabled prompt recording and expects resumed sessions to reuse the cache or preserved thinking.
quote: a different `append` or custom prompt on a resumed session reaches Claude on the next turn, and that request can't reuse the session's [prompt cache](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching.md#how-the-cache-is-organized). Where the API enforces [preserved thinking](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/preserved-thinking), Claude also loses its thinking from earlier turns.

claim: The Python Agent SDK does not accept an array as a custom system prompt.
why: The TypeScript SDK's array form lets callers mark a boundary between static and per-request text.
check: If a Python runner expects a prompt array to preserve its cached static text, check whether its system_prompt input uses a supported form.
quote: The array form isn't available in the Python SDK; [`ClaudeAgentOptions`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/python#claudeagentoptions) lists the forms `system_prompt` accepts.

claim: Anthropic recommends giving each Agent SDK tenant its own filesystem and setting both settingSources: [] and CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1.
why: Filesystem isolation does not prevent the SDK from fetching server-managed settings when the configuration is eligible and the session authenticates with a qualifying credential.
check: For a multi-tenant SDK runner, check the filesystem boundary, settingSources and the auto-memory environment setting together.
quote: For multi-tenant deployments, run each tenant in its own filesystem and set `settingSources: []` plus `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1` in `env`.

claim: The TypeScript Agent SDK supports programmatic hook events that Python lacks, including SessionStart, SessionEnd, TeammateIdle and TaskCompleted.
why: An SDK hook callback can run only for events supported by that language's SDK.
check: If a Python runner relies on one of these events, check whether it uses a filesystem hook or a TypeScript callback.
quote: The TypeScript SDK supports additional hook events beyond Python, including `SessionStart`, `SessionEnd`, `TeammateIdle`, and `TaskCompleted`.

claim: The built-in Explore and Plan subagents can omit agentId from the Agent result needed for an SDK resume.
why: Programmatic resume depends on extracting agentId from the earlier tool result.
check: If a runner needs to resume subagents reliably, check whether it uses a custom or general-purpose agent instead of Explore or Plan.
quote: The built-in [`Explore` and `Plan` agents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents#built-in-subagents) can leave the ID out of that text, so use a custom agent or `general-purpose` when you need to resume.

claim: Since Claude Code v2.1.210, the scan of a subagent's final message prepends a [harness: ...] line for harness-only tags or permission-configuration mentions, while turn markers alone add no such line.
why: The marker names the matched patterns, and permission-configuration references stay as written.
check: Check that parsers for subagent reports tolerate the marker line when a report mentions harness tags or permission configuration.
quote: > For a control-tag or permission-configuration match, Claude Code prepends a `[harness: ...]` marker line naming the matched patterns; a turn-marker match doesn't add the marker line. Those are the only modifications the scan makes: it never removes or rewords the subagent's text.

claim: With Claude Opus 5, Claude Code's claude_code preset tells Claude to call Agent only when asked, and a custom prompt or omitted systemPrompt leaves that instruction out.
why: The preset steers Opus 5 toward explicit delegation requests while keeping the Agent tool available.
check: If an Opus 5 runner uses a custom or omitted systemPrompt, check whether its own prompt supplies the intended delegation guidance.
quote:
* **`claude_code` preset**: when the model is Opus 5, Claude Code adds a line to its system prompt telling Claude not to call the Agent tool unless it's asked to. The Agent tool stays available.
* **A custom prompt, or no `systemPrompt`**: Claude Code doesn't build its system prompt, so that line is absent. Add the prompting guide's delegation instruction to your own prompt.

claim: For hook events that support blocking on callback failure, the matcher option is onFailure: "block" in TypeScript Agent SDK v0.3.317+ or on_failure="block" in Python Agent SDK v0.2.177+.
why: The matcher can stop an action on callback failure, while returning {} counts as making no decision.
check: Check the installed SDK version, the event's blocking behavior and whether a guard surfaces failures instead of catching them and returning {}.
quote: To block the action instead, set `onFailure: "block"` in TypeScript or `on_failure="block"` in Python on the matcher. Requires TypeScript Agent SDK v0.3.317 or later, or Python Agent SDK v0.2.177 or later.

claim: Claude Code reopens the existing worktree when --worktree is passed a name that already exists.
why: A reused name can carry forward the prior run's worktree state.
check: Check whether a runner that needs a separate checkout for each run uses distinct worktree names.
quote: If a worktree with the name you pass to `--worktree` already exists, Claude Code opens it instead of creating a new one.

claim: Scheduled runs, including one-off runs, are capped at 100 per account per hour, and runs over the cap wait for the reset.
why: These starts count toward the account's scheduled-run limit, separate from the limit on API fires and other manual starts.
check: If scheduled tasks start late under load, check the account's scheduled runs against the hourly cap.
quote: | Scheduled runs, including one-off runs | 100 per hour | Your account | The run waits until the limit resets |

claim: Run now and reruns of one-off tasks share an account-wide cap of 100 per hour.
why: This account-wide cap applies in addition to the shared per-task cap, and attempts over it fail until the reset.
check: For automation that reruns tasks, check Run now and one-off reruns together when accounting for the account-wide limit.
quote: | **Run now** and setting a one-off task to run again | 100 per hour | Your account | Same |

claim: Routine API fires have an account-wide cap of 100 per hour that is counted separately from Run now.
why: Attempts over the hourly cap fail until it resets.
check: If a pipeline fires routines across multiple tasks, check its account-wide API fire rate as well as its per-task rate.
quote: | API fires | 100 per hour | Your account, counted separately from **Run now** | Same |

claim: Scheduled task runs draw down Claude subscription usage the same way interactive sessions do.
why: The subscription usage limit is separate from hourly run caps, and organizations with usage credits enabled can continue scheduled runs on metered overage.
check: Check whether the schedule leaves room for interactive work within included usage and whether usage credits are enabled if runs must continue after that allowance.
quote: Scheduled tasks draw down subscription usage the same way interactive sessions do.

claim: Custom cron schedules for Claude scheduled tasks are rejected if they run more than once per hour.
why: Custom cron expressions remain subject to the minimum schedule interval.
check: If a task's custom schedule is rejected, check whether the cron expression can trigger more than once per hour.
quote: Expressions that run more often than once per hour are rejected.

claim: A Claude scheduled task set to run exactly on the hour can start several minutes late.
why: The scheduled time at the top of the hour does not guarantee an immediate start.
check: Check whether a task that needs to start close to its scheduled time is set a few minutes past the hour.
quote: * **Runs on the hour**: if you schedule a run exactly on the hour, such as 9:00, it can start several minutes late. To start close to the scheduled time, pick a few minutes past the hour, for example 9:07.

claim: An effective crossSessionInbound: accept rule lets a messaging-enabled claude -p worker receive messages unattended.
why: With acceptance configured, an approval dialog is unnecessary.
check: If a headless worker must receive messages unattended, check which inbound setting applies to the intended sender.
quote: To let a `-p` worker take messages unattended, start it with `crossSessionInbound` set to `accept` in its `--settings` value. An `accept` in your user settings also works but applies to every session you run.

claim: With cross-session messaging enabled, claude -p binds an inbox socket for incoming messages except in bare mode.
why: A bare session has no inbox socket and does not appear in the agent list.
check: If an expected headless recipient is absent from the agent list, check whether it was started in bare mode.
quote: Claude Code binds an inbox socket for a [`claude -p`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless) session like an interactive one, so a long-running `-p` worker can receive messages and appears in the listing. When you start a session in [bare mode](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless.md#start-faster-with-bare-mode), Claude Code doesn't bind the socket, so that session can't receive messages

claim: Same-machine messaging requires Claude Code v2.1.248 or later on Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud's Agent Platform and Microsoft Foundry, or whenever feature-flag fetching is off.
why: Same-machine messages travel over a per-session socket or named pipe without passing through Anthropic servers.
check: If peers are missing on a third-party provider or with feature-flag fetching off, check the Claude Code version before troubleshooting delivery.
quote: including Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, and Microsoft Foundry, and in sessions that run with [feature-flag fetching](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars.md#features-that-need-feature-flag-fetching) off. On those providers, and with flag fetching off, same-machine messaging requires Claude Code v2.1.248 or later.

claim: To reach cloud sessions or sessions on another of your machines, the sending Claude Code session must be connected to Remote Control with an active claude.ai sign-in.
why: Remote messaging travels through Anthropic servers and depends on Remote Control availability.
check: If a cloud or other-machine peer is missing, check the sender's active authentication and Remote Control connection and, for another machine, the receiver's Remote Control status.
quote: from a session that is connected to Remote Control, which needs a claude.ai sign-in as this session's active authentication and the other [Remote Control requirements](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/remote-control.md#requirements).

claim: Claude Code sessions cannot message across a container and its host or between WSL 2 and native Windows on the same computer.
why: Claude Code can still deliver messages between sessions inside the same container.
check: If two local peers cannot reach each other, check whether they are on opposite sides of a container or WSL 2 boundary.
quote: A session inside a container and a session on the host can't reach each other. Two sessions inside the same container can still message each other, including on a [self-hosted runner](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/self-hosted-environments). A session inside WSL 2 and a native Windows session on the same computer can't reach each other either.

claim: A Claude Code inbox socket connection requires an auth line on native Windows, while the line is optional on macOS and Linux, including WSL 2.
why: Native Windows closes a connection that does not start with a valid auth line before delivering any message.
check: When auditing own-session posts, check that Windows senders authenticate on the first line and that any token belongs to the receiving session.
quote:
* **macOS and Linux, including WSL 2**: the line is optional. Claude Code accepts a connection with or without it.
* **Native Windows**: the line is required. Claude Code closes any connection whose first line isn't a valid auth line and delivers nothing from that connection.

claim: Claude Code closes a connection to its cross-session inbox if the connection sends no complete line within 30 seconds.
why: Opening the connection before a slow command finishes can use up the inbox's initial read window.
check: If a hook posts command output, check that it waits until the message is ready before opening the connection.
quote: Open the connection only when the message you're posting is ready. Claude Code closes a connection that hasn't sent a complete line within 30 seconds, so capture a slow command's output first and then open the connection to send it.

claim: claude --bg from an untrusted directory exits with Workspace not trusted if no workspace trust dialog can appear, as in a script.
why: The workspace must already be trusted for a launch that cannot show the trust dialog.
check: Check whether an unattended launcher reports the workspace trust failure and stops waiting for a session that never starts.
quote: Where no dialog can appear, such as in a script, the command exits with a [`Workspace not trusted`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/errors#workspace-not-trusted-when-dispatching-a-background-session) error instead.

claim: Background edits skip worktree isolation for sessions moved from an open terminal, a session or target already in a linked worktree, writes outside the working directory, and non-git directories without a working WorktreeCreate hook.
why: These cases do not get a newly created worktree for the edit.
check: When background sessions share files, check for an existing linked worktree, writes beyond the working directory or a missing or failed WorktreeCreate hook outside git.
quote:
You [moved a session you already had open to the background](#from-inside-a-session) with `←` or `/background`. That session keeps editing files where it was already working
* The session is already inside a linked git worktree,

claim: Setting worktree.bgIsolation to "none" makes background sessions edit the working copy directly without moving into an isolated worktree.
why: This setting is available for repositories where git worktrees are impractical.
check: If concurrent background jobs may touch the same files, check whether the project's worktree.bgIsolation setting disables isolation.
quote: To turn off worktree isolation for a repository where git worktrees are impractical, set [`worktree.bgIsolation`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#worktree-bgisolation) to `"none"`. Background sessions then edit your working copy directly without moving into a worktree first. Add the setting to the project's `.claude/settings.json`:

claim: For code changes in a worktree Claude entered, Claude Code tells the background session to open a draft pull request when the task calls for one.
why: The pull request label then appears on the session row.
check: If a task asks for a pull request from a background worktree, check that the resulting request is a draft.
quote: * **Draft pull request**: Claude opens one when the task calls for it, and the [`#N` label](#pull-request-status) appears on the row.

claim: For code changes in a worktree Claude entered, Claude Code tells the background session to avoid pushing to main or master, force-pushing or merging.
why: These instructions apply when the session is preserving its work before finishing.
check: If a background workflow expects a merge or a push to the default branch, check whether those actions are assigned outside the session.
quote: * **Never**: pushing to `main` or `master`, force-pushing, and merging.

claim: If a background session's Claude-created worktree has uncommitted changes, claude rm keeps both the worktree and the session row.
why: Preserving the dirty worktree leaves its edits available after the removal attempt.
check: If a cleanup script uses claude rm, check that it handles a session that remains listed because its worktree is dirty.
quote: * `claude rm` keeps it, along with the session row, when it has uncommitted changes.

claim: Claude Code refuses to delete a background session in agent view or with claude rm if its worktree has unpushed commits.
why: The unpushed commits must be accounted for before the session can be removed through these interfaces.
check: Before removing a background session, check whether its worktree contains commits that were never pushed.
quote: One reason Claude Code refuses to delete a session is [unpushed commits in its worktree](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/errors.md#worktree-has-commits-that-are-not-pushed-anywhere). To keep those commits, push them before you delete the session.

claim: Deleting a background session through agent view or claude rm leaves its saved transcript available to claude --resume.
why: The session's list entry and conversation transcript are stored separately.
check: If a workflow deletes a session expecting to erase its conversation, check whether the original session ID can still resume the transcript.
quote: Delete a session with `Ctrl+X` twice in [agent view](#organize-the-list) or with [`claude rm`](#manage-sessions-from-the-shell). The session disappears from the list, unless Claude Code [refuses to delete it](#delete-a-session-after-claude-code-refuses). Its transcript stays on your machine, available through `claude --resume`.

claim: In claude agents --json output, background sessions have state, live processes have status, and waitingFor appears only when status is waiting.
why: A blocked state means the session needs something from you, and waitingFor can be "permission prompt", "input needed", "sandbox request", "worker request" or "dialog open".
check: Check that pollers handle missing status or waitingFor, distinguish working, blocked, done, failed and stopped, and treat busy, waiting and idle as live statuses.
quote:
| `state` | Background sessions | One of `working`, `blocked`, `done`, `failed`, or `stopped`. See [Read session state from a script](#read-session-state-from-a-script) for what each value means |
| `pid`, `status` | While the process is alive | Process ID and one of `busy`, `waiting`, or `idle` |
| `waitingFor` | When `status` is `waiting` |

claim: For dispatch from an agent view opened with the left-arrow key, an auto or bypassPermissions defaultMode takes effect only from managed settings, a --settings file or ~/.claude/settings.json.
why: Project settings cannot supply these two default modes for this dispatch path.
check: If a dispatch depends on auto or bypassPermissions as its default, check that the value comes from an accepted settings source.
quote: `auto` and `bypassPermissions` [take effect only from managed settings, a `--settings` file, or `~/.claude/settings.json`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#permissions-defaultmode).

claim: A background Claude Code session reads settings, including project env values, from the directory it runs in, with any configuration flags carried over from the original session.
why: Project env values in that directory can select the model or provider.
check: If a background runner uses a project model or provider override, check the session's working directory and the env block in the settings it actually loads.
quote: A background session reads its [settings](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings.md) from the directory it runs in, the same as if you had started `claude` there with the [configuration flags it carried over](#what-carries-over-when-you-background). This includes [`env` values](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#env) in project settings,

claim: A background Claude Code session inherits PATH and the cloud provider selection from the shell that dispatched it.
why: Commands in the session find tools on the dispatching shell's PATH.
check: If a background session cannot find a command or uses the wrong cloud provider, check PATH and provider variables in the shell used to dispatch it.
quote: A background session also runs with the `PATH` of the shell you dispatched it from, so the commands it runs find the same tools your terminal does. It keeps that shell's cloud provider selection too, such as `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK` or `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX`

claim: On macOS and Linux, Claude Code background sessions stop if their supervisor stops and no new supervisor connects within about a minute.
why: The supervisor hosts background session processes.
check: If a runner relies on long-lived sessions on macOS or Linux, check whether recovery starts a replacement supervisor within that window.
quote: * **The supervisor itself stops**, for example because its process was ended from outside Claude Code: on macOS and Linux, your sessions stop unless a new supervisor connects within about a minute. To start one, run `claude agents` in your shell. After that minute, see [Keep sessions running after the supervisor stops](#keep-sessions-running-after-the-supervisor-stops).

claim: A stopped Claude Code background session with no saved transcript cannot be resumed, but claude respawn <id> reruns its original prompt.
why: Resuming requires the saved conversation, while a respawn reruns the original prompt.
check: Before retrying a stopped session, check whether its transcript exists and whether restarting the original task would repeat side effects.
quote: When [transcript cleanup](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference.md#cleanupperioddays) has removed a stopped session's saved conversation, Claude Code refuses to open the row: the message says there is nothing to resume. `claude rm <id>` deletes the row, unless [Claude Code refuses](#what-deleting-a-session-removes), and `claude respawn <id>` runs its original prompt again.

claim: A session dispatched with claude --bg or from claude agents started in a shell uses the new-session permission mode for its directory unless agent view dispatch defaults apply.
why: The target directory's new-session permission rules govern an ordinary shell dispatch.
check: If a shell-dispatched worker starts in an unexpected permission mode, check the target directory's settings and any permission mode passed as a dispatch default.
quote: **Dispatched from `claude agents` started in a shell, or with `claude --bg`**: the new session starts the way a new `claude` session in that directory would, unless you dispatched it from an agent view you opened with [dispatch defaults](#dispatch-defaults).
